LATCH: a load-sequence-sensing, any-angle stance-control knee joint for KAFOs — design and validation report

Design package and analysis report

October 2026

Abstract

People with quadriceps paralysis (polio survivors, incomplete spinal-cord injury, stroke) usually walk in knee–ankle–foot orthoses (KAFOs) whose knee is locked straight for the whole gait cycle, forcing hip hiking, circumduction and vaulting. Stance-control knee joints that free the knee in swing cost US$1,700–3,500 per joint and the only purely mechanical ones either need a cable from the ankle or a gravity pendulum that locks only at full extension. We asked whether a knee joint can decide stance from swing using only the loads it already carries. Using a public multi-speed walking dataset (51 subjects, 381 treadmill trials, 0.34–2.23 m/s) we first showed that any pendulum trigger mounted on the thigh is corrupted by the knee’s own accelerations (up to 14 m/s2^2 at toe-off), so that no pendulum length, mount height or damping achieved both reliable locking at heel strike and release before swing. We then designed a joint in which a fine-pitch ratchet (3.75∘^\circ resolution, locks at any knee angle) is engaged and released by the sign sequence of the external knee moment: a flexion load on the pawls sets a mechanical latch, a subsequent extension load on a sprung hyperextension stop releases the pawls, a friction drag ring on the knee axle keeps them lifted while the knee flexes in swing and drops them during swing extension, and two rotary dampers and a dashpot provide the required 0.1–0.3 s time constants. Simulated on 9,781 valid strides with a causal state machine driven by measured knee kinematics and inverse-dynamics moments, the design locked at heel strike in 99.2% of strides at speeds ≤\le1.5 m/s, was unlocked while a buckling load was present in 0.27%, falsely blocked swing flexion in 0.23%, released before pre-swing flexion in 89.6% and never released in 3.6% (a safe, stiff-knee stride). The knee angle at heel strike in the dataset was 7.4±6.0∘7.4\pm6.0^\circ (64% of strides >5∘>5^\circ), which quantifies why single-notch full-extension locks fail. The complete joint is modelled parametrically (22 components, STEP and STL supplied): a laser-cut steel load path (two phased toothed clevis plates, 3-tooth hook pawls, 12 mm pin) with 3D-printed control parts, bill of materials US$74, plane-stress FE peak tooth stress 250–280 MPa at the 70 N⋅\cdotm design moment and 540–600 MPa at a 150 N⋅\cdotm proof moment (17-4PH H900 yield 1,170 MPa). We give the full validation protocol for bench and gait-laboratory testing.

Introduction

The problem

Between 12 and 20 million people live with the paralytic consequences of poliomyelitis, and in the countries that reached full vaccination coverage only after 1988 most of them are still children or young adults [1, 2]. Spinal-cord injury adds 20.6 million prevalent cases worldwide, most of them incomplete [3], and 40–60% of stroke survivors show knee hyperextension in stance because they cannot control the knee [4]. When the quadriceps cannot hold the knee, the standard orthotic answer is a knee–ankle–foot orthosis (KAFO) with a drop lock: the knee is held straight through the whole gait cycle. The locked knee is stable but forces an energy-inefficient long-leg gait (hip hiking, circumduction, vaulting), and long-term use is associated with hip and lumbar compensations and skin damage [5, 6]. Device abandonment is common across assistive technology (29% overall [7]); in a cohort of 98 polio survivors 24% had stopped using their custom KAFO [8]. Globally only about one person in ten who needs prosthetic or orthotic services has access to them, and two to four times more people need orthoses than prostheses [9, 10]; users in Sierra Leone and Malawi rank safety and uneven-ground walking among their main complaints [11].

Stance-control joints and why they are rare

Stance-control knee–ankle–foot orthoses (SCKAFOs) lock the knee only while the leg bears weight and free it in swing. They normalise kinematics reliably even if the energy-cost benefit is modest [12, 13, 14, 6]. Commercial joints fall into three families. (i) Cable-released joints (Ottobock FreeWalk, Becker UTX/Stride family) unlock when the ankle dorsiflexes in late stance and lock only when the knee reaches full extension [6]; (ii) the Fillauer Swing Phase Lock (SPL2) uses an internal gravity pendulum that drops a pawl into a single notch at full extension when the thigh is inclined forward [15]; (iii) sensor-based electromechanical and microprocessor joints (E-MAG, NEURO TRONIC, C-Brace) that cost from €10,000 to US$37,000 as finished orthoses and still show 10–14% unlock failures per step under challenging conditions [16, 17, 18]. Bare mechanical joint systems list at about US$1,700 (FreeWalk kit) to £3,500 (SPL2) [19, 20]. The recurring engineering limitation identified by Yakimovich et al. is “dependence on specific joint angles to switch between stance and swing modes” [6]: a user who falls short of full extension in terminal swing is left unsupported [21]. Becker markets the SafetyStride specifically as resisting flexion at any angle [22]; research joints with any-angle capability have used hydraulics (69 N⋅\cdotm [23]), a linear piston resisting >150>150 N⋅\cdotm [24], a quasi-passive spring clutch [25], a three-tooth 10∘^\circ-pitch ratchet [21], and most recently a low-cost solenoid-driven serrated ring [26]. None of these is simultaneously any-angle, electronics-free, cable-free, pendulum-free and open.

Contribution

This report presents LATCH (Load-Actuated, Thigh-Cable-free, any-angle stance-Control Hinge), a KAFO knee joint that decides stance from swing using only the external knee moment it already carries, with no pendulum, cable, battery or sensor. Three things are new. First, a data-driven negative result that motivates the design: driven by the measured kinematics of 51 subjects, a thigh-mounted pendulum cannot be made reliable at any length, mount height or damping (Section 3.1). Second, a load-sequence stance detector that is realisable with two springs, a friction ring, two rotary dampers and a dashpot, and whose per-stride performance we quantify on 9,781 strides across eight speeds (Section 3.2). Third, a complete parametric design package (CAD, finite-element sizing, bill of materials, assembly and validation protocol) that uses laser-cut steel for the load path and 3D printing for the control mechanism, at a parts cost of US$74 (Sections 4–5).

Methods

Gait data

We used the Fukuchi et al. public walking dataset [27] (“WBDS”; figshare 10.6084/m9.figshare.5722711, v3 release containing 51 adult subjects), restricted to its treadmill trials: eight speeds per subject (40–145% of comfortable speed), 30 s each, giving 381 trials with 150 Hz marker trajectories, 300 Hz split-belt force plates and gait-cycle-normalised joint moments from inverse dynamics. From the markers we computed, for the right leg, the thigh inclination from vertical θ\theta (greater trochanter to lateral knee marker), the knee flexion angle (thigh versus shank segments), and the position and acceleration of points on the lateral thigh upright 0–20 cm above the knee axis, after 8 Hz low-pass filtering. Right heel strikes and toe-offs were detected as force-plate contacts validated by the centre of pressure lying within 18 cm of the right heel and ankle markers. Strides with implausible stance fraction (<50%<50\% or >72%>72\% of the cycle) or duration (outside 0.6–2.4 s) were excluded, leaving 9,781 strides from 51 subjects at 0.34–2.23 m/s (mean body mass 67.8 kg). The knee moment curve of each trial (N⋅\cdotm/kg; positive = internal extensor = external flexion load) was mapped onto each stride by percentage of cycle.

Mechanism simulation

Both trigger concepts were simulated as causal state machines sampled at 150 Hz and driven by the measured kinematics and moments. Because the dataset comes from unimpaired walkers whose knees flex 15–20∘^\circ during loading response, we applied a virtual lock: while the pawls are engaged the knee angle presented to the mechanism cannot exceed the angle at engagement (the ratchet permits extension only), which is what the orthosis would enforce. Pawls carrying an external flexion load cannot be lifted (self-holding tooth geometry); they can only be released when that load is zero.

Pendulum trigger.

A physical pendulum of effective length LeffL_\mathrm{eff} and damping ratio ζ\zeta pivots on the thigh upright at height ss above the knee axis and reads its angle ψ\psi relative to the upright: ψ̈=−(g/Leff)[(1+ay/g)sin⁡ϕ+(ax/g)cos⁡ϕ]−2ζωnψ̇−θ̈\ddot\psi = -(g/L_\mathrm{eff})\,[(1+a_y/g)\sin\phi + (a_x/g)\cos\phi] - 2\zeta\omega_n\dot\psi - \ddot\theta, ϕ=ψ+θ\phi=\psi+\theta, with (ax,ay)(a_x,a_y) the measured pivot acceleration and ±35∘\pm35^\circ travel stops. A bistable toggle arms the lock when ψ≤−θL\psi\le-\theta_L and disarms it when ψ≥+θU\psi\ge+\theta_U. We swept Leff∈[3,40]L_\mathrm{eff}\in[3,40] cm, s∈{0,10,20}s\in\{0,10,20\} cm and ζ∈{0.3,0.7,1.5,3}\zeta\in\{0.3,0.7,1.5,3\} with θL=θU=5∘\theta_L=\theta_U=5^\circ.

Load-sequence trigger (LATCH).

The joint has three mechanical inputs: the external flexion moment carried by the engaged pawls; the external extension moment carried by a sprung hyperextension stop with 1 mm of travel before a hard stop; and the direction of knee rotation sensed by a friction-drag ring on the knee axle with a dead band δ\delta. The logic (Fig. 2) is: (1) a pawl load above MpawlM_\mathrm{pawl} sets a LATCH that decays TlatchT_\mathrm{latch} after the pawl unloads (rotary damper); (2) a stop load above MthrM_\mathrm{thr} while LATCH is set, or sustained for longer than TlongT_\mathrm{long} (dashpot timer), lifts the pawls and keeps them lifted while the stop remains loaded; (3) the drag ring holds the pawls lifted while the knee flexes and lets them drop, after a delay tdropt_\mathrm{drop} set by a second rotary damper, once the knee has extended by δ\delta; (4) the ratchet teeth cover knee angles −5∘-5^\circ to 30∘30^\circ, so pawls dropped at larger flexion ride a smooth rim and engage on reaching the toothed sector. Thresholds are per kilogram of body mass and are set on the device by spring preload screws. The design point is Mthr=0.05M_\mathrm{thr}=0.05, Mpawl=0.08M_\mathrm{pawl}=0.08 N⋅\cdotm/kg, Tlatch=0.15T_\mathrm{latch}=0.15 s, Tlong=0.30T_\mathrm{long}=0.30 s, δ=15∘\delta=15^\circ, tdrop=0.10t_\mathrm{drop}=0.10 s, tlift=0.03t_\mathrm{lift}=0.03 s.

Outcome measures (per stride).

Locked at heel strike: pawls engaged at the next heel strike and 20 ms later. Buckling exposure: any instant before the pre-swing flexion onset at which the knee is unlocked while the external flexion moment exceeds 0.05 N⋅\cdotm/kg. False lock: pawls engaged while the knee is flexing in swing. Released in time: pawls released before the knee needs to flex 5∘^\circ beyond its mid-stance minimum. Stiff stride: no release before toe-off (safe failure). We also report the release instant and the ratcheting travel (clicks) per stride.

CAD, structural sizing and finite elements

The joint was modelled parametrically in CadQuery (OCCT kernel); every dimension in this report is a named parameter in cad_knee.py, and STEP and per-part STL files are exported from the same script. Plane-stress linear elasticity (scikit-fem, quadratic triangles, gmsh meshes refined to 0.15 mm at the loaded teeth) was used for the toothed shank plate: the external flexion moment MM was applied as tractions on the three engaged tooth flanks shared 50/30/20% (a conservative allowance for pitch tolerance), with the plate fixed at its bushing seat. Pins, bushings and uprights were sized analytically.

Results

Why a single-notch lock fails and why a pendulum cannot fix it

Knee flexion at heel strike across the 9,781 strides was 7.4±6.0∘7.4\pm6.0^\circ (5th–95th percentile −0.7-0.7 to 18.1∘18.1^\circ); 64% of strides exceeded 5∘^\circ and 28% exceeded 10∘^\circ (Fig. 1A). A lock with a single notch at full extension therefore depends on the orthotist’s alignment and on the user reaching that one angle every step; an any-angle lock removes the dependence.

A gravity pendulum reads the direction of apparent gravity g−ag-a, not of gg. Fig. 1B shows, for one subject at 1.24 m/s, that the forward acceleration of the knee at toe-off (peaks of 9–14 m/s2^2 at the knee, 5–7 m/s2^2 20 cm up the thigh) tilts apparent gravity by 40–55∘^\circ and its deceleration in terminal swing by 20–40∘^\circ, in each case in the direction that mimics the opposite gait phase. Across the full sweep (Fig. 1C and sweep1.csv) the best pendulum for locking (8 cm, 20 cm mount, ζ=3\zeta=3) locked at heel strike in 99.7% of strides but released before swing in only 2.5%; the best for releasing (3 cm at the knee, ζ=0.3\zeta=0.3) released in 84% but engaged the ratchet during swing flexion in 53% of strides. Long pendulums (Leff≥L_\mathrm{eff}\ge 20 cm) remove the thigh-rotation component but sit near resonance with the stride-frequency hip acceleration and miss the 130 ms release window. Slow, heavily damped pendulums are safe but functionally equivalent to a locked knee. This is the mechanism behind the alignment sensitivity reported for pendulum joints [15, 6], and it is a property of inertial sensing at the knee rather than of any particular product.

The load-sequence stance detector

Fig. 2 shows the LATCH logic on a measured stride at 1.03 m/s. The pawls are engaged at heel strike. The initial-contact extension moment (the ground reaction passes in front of the knee for 50–80 ms) loads the stop but LATCH is not set, so nothing happens; during loading response the external flexion moment loads the pawls and sets LATCH; when the ground reaction moves in front of the knee at 23% of the cycle the stop is loaded while LATCH is live and the pawls lift. The knee is now free but rests against the extension stop, which carries an extension moment of 0.3–0.65 N⋅\cdotm/kg through mid-stance: a knee under an external extension moment is self-stable, which is the biomechanical justification of releasing at this instant. At pre-swing the stop unloads and the knee flexes; the drag ring registers 15∘^\circ of flexion within the 100 ms pawl-drop delay and holds the pawls up through swing. At peak swing flexion the knee reverses, the ring releases the pawls after 15∘^\circ of extension, they ride the smooth rim and ratchet over the last 20∘^\circ (median 21.6∘^\circ of ratcheting, about six clicks at 3.75∘^\circ resolution) and the knee arrives at heel strike locked at whatever angle it reached.

Table 1 and Fig. 3 summarise performance. Within the speed range in which KAFO users walk (≤\le1.5 m/s; 7,278 strides, 51 subjects) the joint was locked at heel strike in 99.2% of strides, was exposed to a buckling load while unlocked in 0.27%, falsely blocked swing flexion in 0.23%, released before the knee needed to flex in 89.6%, released late but before toe-off in a further 6.8%, and never released (stiff-knee stride) in 3.6%. The median release instant was 28% of the cycle (5th–95th percentile 7–51%). Above 1.5 m/s performance degrades (locked at heel strike 89–93%, exposure 7–8%) through one specific chain: fast walkers develop a second external flexion moment in pre-swing that keeps the pawls loaded until toe-off, so LATCH is still live when the shank’s deceleration loads the stop in terminal swing and the joint releases just before heel strike. A hypothetical heel-strike impact detector that allowed LATCH to be set only within 0.5 s of heel strike would raise locking above 1.5 m/s to 98.2% and cut exposure to 0.9% at no cost in the envelope (Fig. 3C, lock_sensitivity.json); we list it as the first design iteration.

The sensitivity study (Fig. 3C) gives three design rules. (i) Preload must err high: thresholds 30% too low reduce locking to 93.6% and raise exposure to 5.3%, whereas thresholds 30% too high keep 99.99% locking and 0.07% exposure at the price of 7.5% stiff strides; the preload screws should therefore be set from the user’s body mass and then backed off only until swing release is observed. (ii) The dashpot timer is essential: without it, strides whose loading-response flexion moment never exceeds MpawlM_\mathrm{pawl} (all slow walking, where the ground reaction stays in front of the knee) never release and 44% of envelope strides are stiff. (iii) The drag-ring dead band and pawl-drop delay are forgiving over δ=10\delta=10–20∘20^\circ and tdrop=60t_\mathrm{drop}=60–150 ms, and a 0.3 N⋅\cdotm/kg, 25 ms stop impulse at terminal swing (shank hitting the extension stop) changes nothing because LATCH is not live at that instant. Knee moment peaks in the dataset were 0.21 (median), 0.82 (95th) and 1.06 N⋅\cdotm/kg (99th percentile) in flexion and 0.51/0.78 N⋅\cdotm/kg in extension, which fixes the structural loads below.

Mechanical design

Load path

The joint attaches to standard 16 mm KAFO uprights. The shank side is a clevis of two 5 mm laser-cut steel plates whose hubs (34 mm tip radius) each carry eight ratchet teeth of 7.5∘^\circ pitch and 3.5 mm depth over knee angles −5∘-5^\circ to +30∘+30^\circ; the outer plate’s teeth are phased by half a pitch, so that with one pawl per plate the knee locks at 3.75∘^\circ intervals while every tooth has the full 7.5∘^\circ root. The remaining rim is at tooth-tip radius, so a pawl dropped at large flexion rides onto the teeth without a step. The 6 mm thigh plate sits between the clevis plates on a 12 mm shoulder bolt in two flanged bronze bushings. Each pawl is a 5 mm hook with three serrations that match the tooth spaces; its 6 mm pivot pin passes through the thigh plate so that both pawls share one pin and are linked by a 3.5 mm bridge pin through an arc slot in the thigh plate, which the lift yoke drives. The pivot lies about 10∘^\circ inside the line of action of the tooth force, and the flanks are undercut by 0.6∘^\circ, so the lock is self-energising: load pulls the pawl into the teeth and the pawls can only be lifted when the flexion load is zero, which is the self-holding behaviour assumed in the simulation. Hyperextension is taken by a lug on the inner shank plate against the stop lever on the thigh plate: a die spring preloaded to MthrM_\mathrm{thr} allows 1 mm of lever travel to actuate the release and then a hard stop carries the remainder of the moment metal-to-metal.

Control deck (printed)

Above the outer plate a 3 mm deck carries the printed lift yoke (pivoting on the thigh plate, forked over the pawl bridge pin), the spring-steel direction ring (a split friction ring clamped on the outer plate boss whose tab moves 15∘^\circ between two faces of the yoke arm), the printed latch lever (pushed to “set” by the sprung pawl-pin seat when the pawls carry more than MpawlM_\mathrm{pawl}, returned through a 15 mm rotary damper giving TlatchT_\mathrm{latch}), the stop-lever push-rod with its dashpot (TlongT_\mathrm{long}) and the second rotary damper on the yoke axis (tdropt_\mathrm{drop}). The cover carries a three-position selector: LOCK forces the yoke down and blocks the release path (standing, stairs down), FREE holds the yoke up (sitting, cycling), AUTO is the stance-control mode. The whole deck and cover are PA12-CF prints (about 45 g); they transmit only spring and damper forces of a few newtons, which is why printed parts are acceptable here and not in the load path.

Mass and cost

The assembly as modelled has 22 components and a computed mass of 963 g, of which 920 g is steel; the thigh plate and two shank plates are modelled as full discs and can be pocketed to roughly halve that. The bill of materials (latch_knee_bom.csv, 23 lines) totals US$74 at single-unit prices, dominated by laser-cutting of five steel parts (US$44) and the three dampers (US$10), against US$1,700–3,500 for commercial mechanical joints [19, 20].

Structural analysis

Design loads follow from Section 3.2 and the literature: a typical peak external flexion moment of 0.5 N⋅\cdotm/kg (36 N⋅\cdotm for 70 kg) for fatigue, the 99th-percentile 1.0 N⋅\cdotm/kg (70 N⋅\cdotm) as design moment, and 150 N⋅\cdotm as proof moment, the latter matching the Ottawa piston joint that was designed for >150>150 N⋅\cdotm and survived 400,000 cycles [24]. Plane-stress finite elements of the toothed plate (Fig. 6) give a von Mises stress at the loaded tooth roots of 250–280 MPa (99th–99.5th percentile of element stresses) at 70 N⋅\cdotm and 540–600 MPa at 150 N⋅\cdotm, with a sharp-corner singular maximum of 570 and 1,215 MPa respectively that a 0.4 mm root fillet removes. For 17-4PH H900 (yield 1,170 MPa, fully reversed fatigue limit about 550 MPa) or through-hardened 1095 this gives a yield safety factor of 2.0 at the proof moment and a fatigue safety factor above 3 at the typical load (root stress about 140 MPa). The analytical checks are: tooth tangential force 2,170 N at 70 N⋅\cdotm; 6 mm pawl pin in double shear 38 MPa, bearing in the 6 mm thigh plate 60 MPa (129 MPa at proof); 12 mm knee pin resultant 3.1 kN, bronze bushing bearing 52 MPa per plate (93 MPa at proof); 16×\times6 mm thigh upright in sagittal bending 273 MPa if one upright carries the full 70 N⋅\cdotm (137 MPa when shared). The FE result also explains why the load path cannot be printed: FFF polyamide-12 and polycarbonate have fatigue limits of 7.4 and 3.6 MPa [28] and even short-carbon-fibre polyamide reaches only 40–117 MPa in tension [29], two orders of magnitude below the tooth-root stress.

Discussion

What the simulation does and does not show

The simulation is a kinematic/kinetic replay: real knee angles and inverse-dynamics moments of unimpaired walkers drive a causal model of the mechanism, with the knee angle clamped while the lock is engaged. It therefore tests the decision logic against the full variability of 51 people at eight speeds, which no bench test can do, but it does not model how a KAFO user’s hip and trunk would adapt to the joint, nor the compliance of the orthosis shells, nor friction and wear. Three systematic differences from a KAFO user should bias the results in a known direction. Quadriceps-weak users keep the ground reaction in front of the knee by trunk lean and hyperextension, so their stance moment is extension-dominated: the latch path fires less often and the timer path more often, which the slow-speed rows of Table 1 already represent. Their swing is slower and lower, which lengthens the pre-swing window and favours release in time. Their knee hits the extension stop at terminal swing, which the impulse test covers. The one chain that limits fast-walking performance (pre-swing flexion load keeping LATCH live into terminal swing) is specific to vigorous push-off and is unlikely in the target population, but the heel-strike gate that removes it is a cheap addition (an inertia latch on the shank).

Comparison with existing joints

Relative to the pendulum SPL2 the design removes the inertial sensing whose failure we quantified, and relative to the cable-released FreeWalk/UTX family it removes the ankle linkage, so it can be fitted to any KAFO including those with a rigid ankle. Relative to the solenoid joint of Wood and Farris [26] and the microprocessor joints it needs no battery. Its 3.75∘^\circ lock resolution is finer than the 10∘^\circ ratchet of the RESNA prototype [21] and comparable to the 2∘^\circ engagement of the Ottawa piston [24]. The release instant (median 28% of the cycle) is earlier than the heel-off release of cable joints; it is biomechanically justified because the external moment is extension from that instant, but it means the user relies on the extension stop rather than the pawls for the second half of stance, exactly as with every other stance-control joint. The 0.27% exposure figure is the fraction of strides in which a flexion load appeared while the pawls were up; in all of these the pawls were already dropping (100 ms delay) and the uncaught flexion in the donor data never exceeded 13∘^\circ.

Limitations and next steps

The CAD is a detailed concept: springs, dampers and the dashpot are modelled as envelopes with specified characteristics, the plates are un-pocketed, and the 963 g mass must be reduced. The FE is two-dimensional and omits the pawl (sized analytically) and contact; a 3D contact model with a root fillet is the next analysis step. The validation protocol is: (1) static proof test to 150 N⋅\cdotm and ultimate test to failure on an ISO 10328-style rig [30], with strain gauges on the pawl and stop lever to calibrate the two preloads; (2) 400,000-cycle fatigue test at 36 N⋅\cdotm with lock–release cycling; (3) bench replay of the WBDS strides on a two-link knee simulator with a programmable moment actuator, which reproduces the exact inputs of this report; (4) gait-laboratory testing with KAFO users on level ground, ramps and stairs with the selector in AUTO and LOCK, measuring lock timing from joint instrumentation and comparing hip hiking, circumduction and oxygen cost with the users’ own locked KAFOs, as in [13, 12]; (5) field evaluation in an LMIC P&O service, where laser cutting and FFF printing are available and the US$74 parts cost matters most.

Conclusion

A knee joint can tell stance from swing from the loads it carries. Driven by 9,781 measured strides, the load-sequence logic locks at heel strike in 99.2% of strides at the speeds KAFO users walk and leaves the knee unprotected under a flexion load in 0.27%, without any pendulum, cable, battery or sensor, and it locks at whatever angle the knee reaches rather than at one alignment-dependent notch. The same data show why gravity pendulums at the knee cannot be made reliable. The design package (parametric CAD, FE sizing, bill of materials at US$74, validation protocol) is released so that the next step, a physical prototype on a bench and then on users, can start immediately.

Data and code availability

Gait data: Fukuchi et al. [27], figshare 10.6084/m9.figshare.5722711. All analysis code is supplied: gait_pipeline.py (event detection and kinematics), sim_trigger.py (pendulum model), sim_lock.py (load-sequence state machine), cad_knee.py (parametric CAD, STEP/STL export), fea_ratchet.py (plane-stress FE), make_figures.py; result tables strides_design.csv, sweep1.csv, sweep_seq.csv, lock_results.json, lock_sensitivity.json, fea_results.json; CAD latch_knee_assembly.step, latch_knee_stl_parts.zip; literature base references.csv (137 verified entries) and evidence_summary.md.
